claim: The nuclear pore complex (NPC) mediates nucleocytoplasmic transport through the nuclear envelope.
source: The nuclear pore complex (NPC) mediates nucleocytoplasmic transport through the nuclear envelope.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about NPC function.

claim: Intermediates of NPC assembly were dome-shaped evaginations of the inner nuclear membrane (INM).
source: Intermediates were dome-shaped evaginations of the inner nuclear membrane (INM), that grew in diameter and depth until they fused with the flat outer nuclear membrane.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by electron tomography data shown in figures.

claim: INM evaginations grew in diameter and depth until they fused with the flat outer nuclear membrane.
source: Intermediates were dome-shaped evaginations of the inner nuclear membrane (INM), that grew in diameter and depth until they fused with the flat outer nuclear membrane.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 2.

claim: Assembly intermediates initially contained the nuclear and cytoplasmic ring component Nup107.
source: Live and super-resolved fluorescence microscopy revealed the molecular maturation of the intermediates, which initially contained the nuclear and cytoplasmic ring component Nup107, and only later the cytoplasmic filament component Nup358.
evidence: This is supported by live imaging and STED microscopy data shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Assembly intermediates only later contained the cytoplasmic filament component Nup358.
source: Live and super-resolved fluorescence microscopy revealed the molecular maturation of the intermediates, which initially contained the nuclear and cytoplasmic ring component Nup107, and only later the cytoplasmic filament component Nup358.
evidence: This is supported by kinetic analysis and STED microscopy data shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: The evagination base was surrounded by an 8-fold rotationally symmetric ring structure from the beginning.
source: EM particle averaging showed that the evagination base was surrounded by an 8-fold rotationally symmetric ring structure from the beginning and that a growing mushroom-shaped density was continuously associated with the deforming membrane.
evidence: This is supported by particle averaging analysis shown in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: A growing mushroom-shaped density was continuously associated with the deforming membrane.
source: EM particle averaging showed that the evagination base was surrounded by an 8-fold rotationally symmetric ring structure from the beginning and that a growing mushroom-shaped density was continuously associated with the deforming membrane.
evidence: This is supported by particle averaging analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: Interphase NPC assembly proceeds by an asymmetric inside-out extrusion of the INM.
source: Quantitative structural analysis revealed that interphase NPC assembly proceeds by an asymmetric inside-out extrusion of the INM.
evidence: This is the main conclusion supported by the combined structural and quantitative analysis presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The NPC is the largest non-polymeric protein complex in eukaryotic cells.
source: The nuclear pore complex (NPC) is the largest non-polymeric protein complex in eukaryotic cells, embedded in a double membrane called the nuclear envelope (NE), and mediates all macromolecular transport across the NE.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge cited in the introduction.

claim: The NPC has an octameric structure and is composed of multiple copies of over 30 different proteins termed nucleoporins (Nups).
source: The NPC has an octameric structure and is composed of multiple copies of over 30 different proteins termed nucleoporins (Nups) (Grossman et al., 2012; Schwartz, 2013; Strambio-De-Castillia et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: In metazoan cells NPCs are assembled in two cell-cycle stages: during nuclear assembly post anaphase and during nuclear growth in interphase.
source: In metazoan cells NPCs are assembled in two cell-cycle stages, during nuclear assembly post anaphase and during nuclear growth in interphase.
evidence: This is established knowledge about NPC assembly pathways.

claim: Postmitotic formation of import competent nuclei with sealed nuclear membranes and functional NPCs is completed very rapidly within 15 min after anaphase onset.
source: In postmitotic assembly, the double nuclear membrane and the NPC channel assemble concomitantly onto chromatin, and postmitotic formation of import competent nuclei with sealed nuclear membranes and functional NPCs is completed very rapidly within 15 min after anaphase onset (Dultz et al., 2008; Haraguchi et al., 2000; Lu et al., 2011; Otsuka et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Interphase NPC assembly occurs only after the NE is fully sealed in late anaphase.
source: By contrast, interphase NPC assembly occurs only after the NE is fully sealed in late anaphase.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the timing of interphase assembly.

claim: Interphase assembly is much slower compared to postmitotic assembly.
source: Interphase assembly is much slower compared to postmitotic assembly and shows differences in the molecular requirements and the order of recruited components (D'Angelo et al., 2006; Dultz and Ellenberg, 2010; Schellhaus et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Studies using in vitro assembled nuclei with Xenopus egg extracts have shown the requirement of RanGTP on both sides of the NE.
source: Studies using in vitro assembled nuclei with Xenopus egg extracts have shown the requirement of RanGTP on both sides of the NE (D'Angelo et al., 2006) and the import of Nup153 to recruit the Nup107-160 complex to the INM (Vollmer et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to D'Angelo et al., 2006.

claim: The import of Nup153 recruits the Nup107-160 complex to the INM.
source: Studies using in vitro assembled nuclei with Xenopus egg extracts have shown the requirement of RanGTP on both sides of the NE (D'Angelo et al., 2006) and the import of Nup153 to recruit the Nup107-160 complex to the INM (Vollmer et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vollmer et al., 2015.

claim: In mammalian cells, the membrane curvature-sensing domain of Nup133 is required for interphase assembly.
source: In mammalian cells, the membrane curvature-sensing domain of Nup133 (Doucet et al., 2010), the INM protein Sun1 (Talamas and Hetzer, 2011), and the targeting of the transmembrane nucleoporin Pom121 to the INM (Funakoshi et al., 2011) have been reported to be required.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Doucet et al., 2010.

claim: The INM protein Sun1 is required for interphase NPC assembly in mammalian cells.
source: In mammalian cells, the membrane curvature-sensing domain of Nup133 (Doucet et al., 2010), the INM protein Sun1 (Talamas and Hetzer, 2011), and the targeting of the transmembrane nucleoporin Pom121 to the INM (Funakoshi et al., 2011) have been reported to be required.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Talamas and Hetzer, 2011.

claim: The targeting of the transmembrane nucleoporin Pom121 to the INM is required for interphase NPC assembly in mammalian cells.
source: In mammalian cells, the membrane curvature-sensing domain of Nup133 (Doucet et al., 2010), the INM protein Sun1 (Talamas and Hetzer, 2011), and the targeting of the transmembrane nucleoporin Pom121 to the INM (Funakoshi et al., 2011) have been reported to be required.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Funakoshi et al., 2011.

claim: INM deformations have been observed in yeast mutants lacking several nucleoporins, membrane proteins Apq12 and Brr6, and the AAA-ATPase VPS4.
source: Interestingly, INM deformations have been observed in yeast mutants lacking several nucleoporins, membrane proteins Apq12 and Brr6, and the AAA-ATPase VPS4 and, while sometimes interpreted as pleiotropic consequences of transport defects, have also been suggested to be involved in nucleoporin quality control or NPC assembly (Chadrin et al., 2010; Hodge et al., 2010; Makio et al., 2009; Meszaros et al., 2015; Murphy et al., 1996; Scarcelli et al., 2007; Webster et al., 2014; Wente and Blobel, 1993).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Core regions result from the so called 'core regions' where nuclear membrane sealing is locally delayed in mitosis due to removal of dense spindle microtubules from the DNA surface.
source: These islands result from the so called 'core regions' where nuclear membrane sealing is locally delayed in mitosis due to removal of dense spindle microtubules from the DNA surface (Vietri et al., 2015) and therefore largely devoid of postmitotic NPC assembly, resulting in a low NPC density in the membrane of the core regions (Dechat et al., 2004; Haraguchi et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Vietri et al., 2015.

claim: Core regions are largely devoid of postmitotic NPC assembly, resulting in a low NPC density.
source: These islands result from the so called 'core regions' where nuclear membrane sealing is locally delayed in mitosis due to removal of dense spindle microtubules from the DNA surface (Vietri et al., 2015) and therefore largely devoid of postmitotic NPC assembly, resulting in a low NPC density in the membrane of the core regions (Dechat et al., 2004; Haraguchi et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dechat et al., 2004 and Haraguchi et al., 2000.

claim: Approximately 50 nm evaginations of the INM were consistently found in 158 tomograms.
source: In the resulting 158 tomograms, we consistently found approximately 50 nm evaginations of the INM (Figure 1B, Table 1, and Video 1) filled with electron dense material, that were clearly distinct from the ~200 nm nuclear egress structures transporting ribonucleoproteins and viruses reported recently (Mettenleiter et al., 2013; Speese et al., 2012).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by data in Table 1 and Figure 1B.

claim: The evaginations were filled with electron dense material.
source: In the resulting 158 tomograms, we consistently found approximately 50 nm evaginations of the INM (Figure 1B, Table 1, and Video 1) filled with electron dense material, that were clearly distinct from the ~200 nm nuclear egress structures transporting ribonucleoproteins and viruses reported recently (Mettenleiter et al., 2013; Speese et al., 2012).
evidence: This is directly observed in electron tomography images.

claim: The evaginations were clearly distinct from the ~200 nm nuclear egress structures transporting ribonucleoproteins and viruses.
source: In the resulting 158 tomograms, we consistently found approximately 50 nm evaginations of the INM (Figure 1B, Table 1, and Video 1) filled with electron dense material, that were clearly distinct from the ~200 nm nuclear egress structures transporting ribonucleoproteins and viruses reported recently (Mettenleiter et al., 2013; Speese et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on size comparison and citations to previous studies.

claim: Immuno-EM showed that the evaginations were specifically enriched with at least one of the nucleoporins recognized by mAb414 (Nup62, Nup153, Nup214, and Nup358).
source: Immuno-EM showed that the evaginations were specifically enriched with at least one of the nucleoporins recognized by mAb414 (Nup62, Nup153, Nup214, and Nup358) (Figure 1C,D, and Figure 1—figure supplement 3A), suggesting that they are pore assembly intermediates.
evidence: This is supported by immuno-EM data shown in Figure 1C,D.

claim: 31 gold particles were found on 13 intermediates in immuno-EM, whereas random distribution estimated 1.6 particles on 13 intermediates.
source: 31 particles were found on 13 intermediates, whereas the random distribution estimated 1.6 particles to be on 13 intermediates. The p-value (probability that the distribution is due to chance alone) <10–100; a chi-square goodness of fit test.
evidence: This is quantitative data from immuno-EM analysis shown in Figure 1D with statistical testing.

claim: Similar INM evaginations filled with electron dense material were found in cryo-electron tomograms of vitrified isolated NEs.
source: Similar INM evaginations filled with electron dense material were also found in cryo-electron tomograms of vitrified isolated NEs (Figure 1E), ruling out that they are artifacts of dehydration, heavy metal staining or resin-embedding during cryo-substitution, and demonstrating that they are stable membrane structures that persist even after in vitro isolation of the NE (Bui et al., 2013; Ori et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by cryo-EM data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The evaginations are not artifacts of dehydration, heavy metal staining or resin-embedding during cryo-substitution.
source: Similar INM evaginations filled with electron dense material were also found in cryo-electron tomograms of vitrified isolated NEs (Figure 1E), ruling out that they are artifacts of dehydration, heavy metal staining or resin-embedding during cryo-substitution, and demonstrating that they are stable membrane structures that persist even after in vitro isolation of the NE (Bui et al., 2013; Ori et al., 2013).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of similar structures in cryo-EM.

claim: Indistinguishable evaginations of the INM were observed in U2OS (human bone osteosarcoma epithelial) and NRK (normal rat kidney) cells.
source: Indistinguishable evaginations of the INM were also observed in U2OS (human bone osteosarcoma epithelial) and NRK (normal rat kidney) cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B), ruling out that their occurrence is cell type, cancer or species specific.
evidence: This is supported by EM data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Evagination depth increased significantly from 16 to 22 nm within 9 min (19 to 28 min post anaphase).
source: Quantitative analysis of 135 INM evagination membrane profiles from a time course of cells captured at 19, 28, and 53 min post anaphase revealed that evaginations progressively grow inside-out (Figure 2). Evagination depth increased significantly from 16 to 22 nm within 9 min (19 to 28 min post anaphase; Figure 2C) and evagination diameter continuously and significantly increased from 51 to 58 nm within 34 min (19 to 53 min post anaphase; Figure 2D).
evidence: This is quantitative data from membrane profile analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Evagination diameter continuously and significantly increased from 51 to 58 nm within 34 min (19 to 53 min post anaphase).
source: Quantitative analysis of 135 INM evagination membrane profiles from a time course of cells captured at 19, 28, and 53 min post anaphase revealed that evaginations progressively grow inside-out (Figure 2). Evagination depth increased significantly from 16 to 22 nm within 9 min (19 to 28 min post anaphase; Figure 2C) and evagination diameter continuously and significantly increased from 51 to 58 nm within 34 min (19 to 53 min post anaphase; Figure 2D).
evidence: This is quantitative data from membrane profile analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Among 279 total evaginations found in 154 µm2 NE surface area, only five ONM/INM fusion events were captured.
source: Among the 279 total evaginations we found in 154 µm2 NE surface area (Table 1), we capture only five ONM/INM fusion events (Figure 2), where the INM evagination had reached the flat ONM surface.
evidence: This is quantitative data summarized in Table 1.

claim: Fusion intermediates had an average evagination depth of 28 nm, similar to the ONM/INM distance.
source: These fusion intermediates had an average evagination depth of 28 nm, similar to the ONM/INM distance and an average diameter of 61 nm, intermediate between late evaginations and mature nuclear pores (Figure 2C,D), as expected for NPC assembly.
evidence: This is quantitative data from membrane profile analysis shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: Fusion intermediates had an average diameter of 61 nm, intermediate between late evaginations and mature nuclear pores.
source: These fusion intermediates had an average evagination depth of 28 nm, similar to the ONM/INM distance and an average diameter of 61 nm, intermediate between late evaginations and mature nuclear pores (Figure 2C,D), as expected for NPC assembly.
evidence: This is quantitative data from membrane profile analysis shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: The low number of fusion intermediates indicates that the fusion step must be very short-lived.
source: The low number of fusion intermediates indicates that the fusion step must be very short-lived.
evidence: This is inferred from the rarity of fusion intermediates observed.

claim: Assembly intermediates are most abundant in core regions during the first hour, when this sealed membrane area still has a low density of mature pores.
source: This data showed that assembly intermediates are most abundant in core regions during the first hour, when this sealed membrane area still has a low density of mature pores due to the lack of postmitotic assembly (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Non-core regions already exhibited a high density of mature pores that arose from postmitotic NPC assembly.
source: By contrast and as expected, non-core regions already exhibited a high density of mature pores that arose from postmitotic NPC assembly (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Later than one hour post anaphase, the ratio of assembly intermediates to mature pores in the core regions had equilibrated to a similar level as found in non-core regions or fully grown nuclei.
source: Later than one hour post anaphase, the ratio of assembly intermediates to mature pores in the core regions had equilibrated to a similar level as found in non-core regions or fully grown nuclei (Figure 3A,B), indicating that a period of frequent interphase pore assembly events during the first hour of G1 nuclear expansion populates the core regions of the NE with NPCs until the steady state interphase density is reached.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: The typical maturation time for interphase assembly is 44 min (95% confidence interval [41‒50]).
source: For the best model, where the majority of intermediates are initiated 10 starting minutes after anaphase onset (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C, Variant 3) we can estimate the typical maturation time for interphase assembly to be 44 min (95% confidence interval [41‒50]).
evidence: This is derived from mathematical modeling of the experimental data.

claim: The obtained maturation time is in good agreement with previous reports based on fluorescence microscopy (~25 min, D'Angelo et al., 2006; ~60 min, Dultz and Ellenberg, 2010).
source: The obtained maturation time is in good agreement with previous reports based on fluorescence microscopy (~25 min, D'Angelo et al., 2006; ~60 min, Dultz and Ellenberg, 2010).
evidence: This compares the current findings with previous studies.

claim: Inside-out evaginations were present at lower density in non-core regions.
source: It is important to note that inside-out evaginations were present at lower density in non-core regions (Figure 3B 'Non-core') and that we found no significant difference in the increase in depth or diameter of evaginations between non-core and core regions during G1 expansion (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figures 2E,F and 3B.

claim: There is no significant difference in the increase in depth or diameter of evaginations between non-core and core regions during G1 expansion.
source: It is important to note that inside-out evaginations were present at lower density in non-core regions (Figure 3B 'Non-core') and that we found no significant difference in the increase in depth or diameter of evaginations between non-core and core regions during G1 expansion (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 2E,F.

claim: Identical evaginating structures were found at low density in fully grown nuclei sampled at later cell-cycle stages.
source: In addition, identical evaginating structures were also found at low density in fully grown nuclei sampled at later cell-cycle stages (Figure 3B 'Mature NE') indicating that the inside-out assembly mechanism is not specific to G1 but occurs throughout interphase.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The inside-out assembly mechanism is not specific to G1 but occurs throughout interphase.
source: In addition, identical evaginating structures were also found at low density in fully grown nuclei sampled at later cell-cycle stages (Figure 3B 'Mature NE') indicating that the inside-out assembly mechanism is not specific to G1 but occurs throughout interphase.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of intermediates in mature nuclei.

claim: The steady state abundance of assembly intermediates in non-core regions and interphase nuclei would be sufficient to maintain the constant NPC density during nuclear growth in interphase.
source: Assuming the maturation time of 44 min, our model shows that the steady state abundance of assembly intermediates we observed in non-core regions and interphase nuclei would be sufficient to maintain the constant NPC density during nuclear growth in interphase that we observed (Figure 3B "model", and Figure 3—figure supplement 1, 2) consistent with previous reports (Dultz and Ellenberg, 2010; Maeshima et al., 2010).
evidence: This is derived from mathematical modeling of the data.

claim: The kinetics of NPC assembly are similar across the nuclear surface and throughout interphase.
source: Taken together these results suggest that the assembly intermediates are present across the NE surface, and that the kinetics of NPC assembly are similar across the nuclear surface and throughout interphase.
evidence: This is inferred from the similarity of intermediate structures and growth kinetics in different regions.

claim: The abundance of intermediates can quantitatively explain both the increase in mature NPCs in the core regions during the rapid nuclear expansion in G1 as well as the homeostatic NPC assembly during nuclear growth later during interphase.
source: Most importantly, the abundance of intermediates can quantitatively explain both the increase in mature NPCs in the core regions during the rapid nuclear expansion in G1 as well as the homeostatic NPC assembly during nuclear growth later during interphase.
evidence: This is derived from mathematical modeling and quantitative analysis of the data.

claim: Nup107, a component of the nuclear and cytoplasmic ring, is recruited very early (t1/2 = 15 min).
source: Kinetic comparison of interphase accumulation of both Nups in the core region clearly revealed that Nup107, a component of the nuclear and cytoplasmic ring, is recruited very early (t1/2 = 15 min, see Materials and methods for details), while Nup358, a component of the cytoplasmic filaments, is recruited only after a significant lag phase (t1/2 = 51 min) (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is derived from kinetic analysis of live imaging data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Nup358, a component of the cytoplasmic filaments, is recruited only after a significant lag phase (t1/2 = 51 min).
source: Kinetic comparison of interphase accumulation of both Nups in the core region clearly revealed that Nup107, a component of the nuclear and cytoplasmic ring, is recruited very early (t1/2 = 15 min, see Materials and methods for details), while Nup358, a component of the cytoplasmic filaments, is recruited only after a significant lag phase (t1/2 = 51 min) (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is derived from kinetic analysis of live imaging data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The kinetically distinct and continuously increasing accumulation of two components of the NPC in the core region strongly support a maturation process of assembly intermediates into full pores.
source: The kinetically distinct and continuously increasing accumulation of two components of the NPC in the core region strongly support a maturation process of assembly intermediates into full pores.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential kinetics of Nup107 and Nup358 accumulation.

claim: The late recruitment of the cytoplasmic Nup358 is consistent with an inside-out assembly mechanism on the molecular level.
source: In addition, the late recruitment of the cytoplasmic Nup358 is consistent with an inside-out assembly mechanism on the molecular level.
evidence: This is inferred from the kinetic data and the known localization of Nup358.

claim: Single NPC intermediates in early G1 cells contain Nup107 but not Nup358.
source: The kinetic analysis of bulk Nup accumulation across the inner-core region predicts that single NPC intermediates in early G1 cells should contain Nup107 but not Nup358.
evidence: This is supported by STED microscopy data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Many pore-sized discrete localizations of Nup107 in optical sections of the inner-core region NE in early G1 cells did not have significant Nup358 labeling.
source: This analysis indeed revealed many pore-sized discrete localizations of Nup107 in optical sections of the inner-core region NE in early G1 cells, which did not have significant Nup358 labeling (Figure 5A,B '24 min, inner-core'), while non-core regions in the same nucleus contained only double labeled localizations with Nup358 appearing on top of the Nup107 labeling on the outside of the NE (Figure 5A,B '24 min, non-core'), indicative of mature pores.
evidence: This is supported by STED microscopy data shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: Non-core regions in early G1 cells contained only double labeled localizations with Nup358 appearing on top of the Nup107 labeling on the outside of the NE, indicative of mature pores.
source: This analysis indeed revealed many pore-sized discrete localizations of Nup107 in optical sections of the inner-core region NE in early G1 cells, which did not have significant Nup358 labeling (Figure 5A,B '24 min, inner-core'), while non-core regions in the same nucleus contained only double labeled localizations with Nup358 appearing on top of the Nup107 labeling on the outside of the NE (Figure 5A,B '24 min, non-core'), indicative of mature pores.
evidence: This is supported by STED microscopy data shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: After G1 expansion, the inner-core region had almost only double-labeled structures, consistent with the maturation of intermediates into mature pores.
source: After G1 expansion, also the inner-core region had almost only double-labeled structures (Figure 5A,B '108 min'), consistent with the maturation of intermediates into mature pores.
evidence: This is supported by STED microscopy data shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: Intermediates are specific to the core region and occur only transiently during the first hour of G1.
source: Quantification of the signal in segments along the NE profile allowed us to estimate the frequency of intermediates by the ratio of Nup107/Nup358 (Figure 5C), showing that they are specific to the core region and occur only transiently during the first hour of G1.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of STED data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Cytoplasmic nucleoporins such as Nup358 are only recruited at the end of the maturation process, presumably after the growing INM evagination has fused with the ONM.
source: These results are fully consistent with the EM observations that interphase NPC assembly intermediates populate the core region of NEs with an abundance that matches the number of mature pores found in this region an hour later after nuclear expansion (Figure 3A,B), and suggest that cytoplasmic nucleoporins such as Nup358 are only recruited at the end of the maturation process, presumably after the growing INM evagination has fused with the ONM.
evidence: This is inferred from the late recruitment kinetics of Nup358 and the inside-out assembly mechanism.

claim: Averaging of 11–36 intermediates revealed a ring structure composed of eight regularly spaced subunits underneath the INM.
source: Averaging of 11–36 intermediates revealed a ring structure composed of eight regularly spaced subunits underneath the INM (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1), which was strikingly similar to the nuclear ring of the mature NPC (compare top views (ii) of the mature pore and intermediates in Figure 6B) (Bui et al., 2013; Maimon et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by particle averaging analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The eight-fold symmetric ring structure underneath the INM was strikingly similar to the nuclear ring of the mature NPC.
source: Averaging of 11–36 intermediates revealed a ring structure composed of eight regularly spaced subunits underneath the INM (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1), which was strikingly similar to the nuclear ring of the mature NPC (compare top views (ii) of the mature pore and intermediates in Figure 6B) (Bui et al., 2013; Maimon et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of averaged structures in Figure 6B and citations.

claim: Eight-fold symmetric rings were already present in the shallowest evaginations detected during early G1.
source: These eight-fold symmetric rings were already present in the shallowest evaginations we could detect during early G1 and could also be seen in individual tomograms (Figure 6A,B, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by particle averaging and individual tomogram data shown in Figure 6A,B.

claim: Side views of the averaged particles revealed a progressive growth of the mushroom-shaped protein density, whose cap closely matched the growing membrane evagination in depth and diameter.
source: Interestingly, side views of the averaged particles revealed a progressive growth also of the mushroom-shaped protein density, whose cap closely matched the growing membrane evagination in depth and diameter and whose stalk was located centrally inside the nuclear ring and grew in length as the cap moved towards the outer membrane (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by particle averaging analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The stalk of the mushroom-shaped density was located centrally inside the nuclear ring and grew in length as the cap moved towards the outer membrane.
source: Interestingly, side views of the averaged particles revealed a progressive growth also of the mushroom-shaped protein density, whose cap closely matched the growing membrane evagination in depth and diameter and whose stalk was located centrally inside the nuclear ring and grew in length as the cap moved towards the outer membrane (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by particle averaging analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The observed INM evaginations represent partially assembled NPCs, which contain minimally the nuclear ring with Nup107 and at least one of the central or nuclear O-glycosylated FG-repeat nucleoporins labeled by mAb414, Nup62 and/or Nup153.
source: Taken together, we can conclude that the observed INM evaginations represent partially assembled NPCs, which contain minimally the nuclear ring with Nup107 and at least one of the central or nuclear O-glycosylated FG-repeat nucleoporins labeled by mAb414, Nup62 and/or Nup153, do not contain Nup358, and are unlikely to contain the cytoplasmic filament base protein Nup214 due to their inside out nature and the lack of Nup358.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined EM, immuno-EM, and fluorescence microscopy data.

claim: The observed INM evaginations do not contain Nup358.
source: Taken together, we can conclude that the observed INM evaginations represent partially assembled NPCs, which contain minimally the nuclear ring with Nup107 and at least one of the central or nuclear O-glycosylated FG-repeat nucleoporins labeled by mAb414, Nup62 and/or Nup153, do not contain Nup358, and are unlikely to contain the cytoplasmic filament base protein Nup214 due to their inside out nature and the lack of Nup358.
evidence: This is supported by STED microscopy data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The observed INM evaginations are unlikely to contain the cytoplasmic filament base protein Nup214 due to their inside out nature and the lack of Nup358.
source: Taken together, we can conclude that the observed INM evaginations represent partially assembled NPCs, which contain minimally the nuclear ring with Nup107 and at least one of the central or nuclear O-glycosylated FG-repeat nucleoporins labeled by mAb414, Nup62 and/or Nup153, do not contain Nup358, and are unlikely to contain the cytoplasmic filament base protein Nup214 due to their inside out nature and the lack of Nup358.
evidence: This is inferred from the inside-out nature of the intermediates and the known association of Nup214 with Nup358.

claim: The first clearly detectable NPC intermediate is a shallow INM evagination surrounded at its base by an 8-fold rotationally symmetric nuclear ring complex.
source: The first clearly detectable NPC intermediate is a shallow INM evagination surrounded at its base by an 8-fold rotationally symmetric nuclear ring complex, in whose center a dome-shaped density with a short stalk is embedded into the INM evagination.
evidence: This is supported by particle averaging analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: In the center of the nuclear ring complex, a dome-shaped density with a short stalk is embedded into the INM evagination.
source: The first clearly detectable NPC intermediate is a shallow INM evagination surrounded at its base by an 8-fold rotationally symmetric nuclear ring complex, in whose center a dome-shaped density with a short stalk is embedded into the INM evagination.
evidence: This is supported by particle averaging analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: The shallow dome matures into a curved mushroom cap, always in direct contact with the growing evagination of the INM and supported by an elongating stalk on the nucleoplasmic side located in the center of the nuclear ring.
source: Subsequently, this shallow dome matures into a curved mushroom cap, always in direct contact with the growing evagination of the INM and supported by an elongating stalk on the nucleoplasmic side located in the center of the nuclear ring.
evidence: This is supported by particle averaging analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: The mushroom-shaped density may use the membrane-attached nuclear ring to determine the site of NPC formation.
source: We speculate that the mushroom-shaped density may use the membrane-attached nuclear ring to determine the site of NPC formation.
evidence: This is speculative interpretation of the structural data.

claim: The mushroom-shaped density, potentially through connections to the nuclear ring, might generate the mechanical force needed for INM deformation and eventual fusion with the ONM.
source: It is further tempting to speculate that the mushroom-shaped density, potentially through connections to the nuclear ring, might generate the mechanical force needed for INM deformation and eventual fusion with the ONM.
evidence: This is speculative interpretation of the structural data.

claim: The mushroom-shaped structure is clearly distinct from the scaffold architecture of the mature NPC.
source: Interestingly, the mushroom-shaped structure is clearly distinct from the scaffold architecture of the mature NPC, indicating that interphase assembly cannot be explained by a simple collection of NPC subcomplexes over time but likely involves major structural rearrangements.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of intermediate and mature NPC structures.

claim: Interphase assembly cannot be explained by a simple collection of NPC subcomplexes over time but likely involves major structural rearrangements.
source: Interestingly, the mushroom-shaped structure is clearly distinct from the scaffold architecture of the mature NPC, indicating that interphase assembly cannot be explained by a simple collection of NPC subcomplexes over time but likely involves major structural rearrangements.
evidence: This is inferred from the distinct structure of intermediates compared to mature NPCs.

claim: This inside-out extrusion mechanism is demonstrated in situ in human cells.
source: Given that it had so far been unclear how interphase NPC assembly occurs, this inside-out extrusion mechanism, demonstrated in situ in human cells, provides a new framework to interpret existing genetic (yeast) and biochemical (Xenopus) data and to investigate the detailed molecular mechanism regulating the assembly process in the future.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on the combined data.

claim: The NPC lifetime is ~40 hr in cells with a similar cell-cycle duration.
source: NPC production and degradation rates were estimated from the measured steady state density of 11 NPCs/µm2 (Figure 3B) and a reported NPC lifetime of ~40 hr in cells with a similar cell-cycle duration (Rabut et al., 2004; Schwanhausser et al., 2011) and are in line with the rare and rapid pore disassembly events that have been observed in mammalian cells (Dultz and Ellenberg, 2010).
